About: Equipotential Surfaces — Always Exactly Perpendicular

Source

Topic
Electrostatics — electric potential & equipotentials
Concept
Field lines meet equipotentials at exactly 90° everywhere — forced by E = −∇V.
Serves
Building geometric intuition for potential vs. field; distinguishing a scalar sum that cancels from a vector that does not.
Inquiry
How much work does it take to move a charge along an equipotential — some, none, or path-dependent?
Misconception
"V = 0 implies E = 0." False. At the dipole midpoint V = 0 exactly, yet |E| is large.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict

You will drag a test charge along an equipotential contour, from one side of the picture to the other. How much work do you have to do against the electric force?

2 · Observe

Drag the pink test charge onto the cyan contour and slide it along the curve. The work counter does not move. Now cut across the contours: it does — up toward higher V, down toward lower V.

The measured angle between E and the contour reads 90.0° wherever you stop.

3 · The midpoint

The cross-hair marks the midpoint of the dipole — equally far from the +q and from the −q. What is true there?

4 · Why 90°, always

Because E = −∇V. The gradient of V points along the direction of steepest change in V; an equipotential is by definition a curve of no change. Those two directions are perpendicular — necessarily, not by artistic choice.

Explore freely: change the sign of q₂, the contour level, and where the test charge sits. The measured angle stays at 90.0° everywhere.

01

At a glance

Two point charges sit on a line, q₁ = +1 on the left and q₂ = ±1 on the right. The sim draws the field lines, one chosen contour of equal potential, and a pink test charge you can move. Two readouts report the result.

What you'll learn

  • What an equipotential contour is, and how a level picks one.
  • What the work counter measures as you drag the test charge.
  • How the field E and the contours are related.
  • What the potential and the field each say at one point.
A contour joins the points that share one value of V. The test charge sits on it.

What's on screen

  • Amber lines are the field lines, with arrows for the direction of E.
  • The cyan contour is the chosen level. Fainter rings are spaced at equal steps of 0.25 in V.
  • The pink test charge, with an amber E arrow and a dashed cyan tangent.
  • Readouts for the angle and the work counter.
See itLook at the scene as it opens. Watch for: a red and a blue charge, a cyan loop round the red one, and a pink dot at the top.

03

A contour joins the points where V has one value

The potential at a point is a plain number: the sum of one term from each charge. It has no direction, and a negative charge contributes a negative term.

V = q₁ / r₁ + q₂ / r₂
r₁ and r₂ are the distances from the point to each charge.
  • The level slider picks one value of V. The bold cyan curve joins every point that has it, and that curve is an equipotential.
  • For the dipole, V = +0.50 is a loop round the positive charge. It crosses the axis at x = −2.236 and x = −0.236.
  • For two like charges at (0, 1.50), each adds 0.5547, so V = 1.109.
  • Two like charges make V positive everywhere in the frame. A level of −0.50 then has no contour, and the sim says so.
See itRaise the level from 0.50 to 1.00. Watch for: the cyan loop shrinking to cross the axis at x = −1.732 and x = −0.414.
04

No work is done moving along an equipotential

Moving a test charge q from A to B takes work equal to q times the change in potential:

W = q (VB − VA) = q ΔV
Along a contour V never changes, so ΔV = 0 and W = 0.
  • The field still pushes on the charge there, but at right angles to each step, so the push does no work.
  • The counter adds q(Vnew − Vold) at every move, with q = +1. It therefore reads Vend − Vstart, whatever route you took.
  • Going from (0, 1.50) to (1.00, 1.50) crosses contours. V changes from 0 to −0.267, so the counter reads −0.267: the field supplies the energy.
See itSlide the charge down the V = 0.50 contour, from y = 1.04 to −1.04 at x = −1.50. Watch for: the work counter staying at 0.000.
See itNow cut across the contours, from x = 0 to x = 1.00 at y = 1.50. Watch for: the counter moving to −0.267.
05

The field is perpendicular to every equipotential

The field is the downhill slope of the potential. A tiny step ds along a contour changes V by zero, and any change in V equals −E·ds:

dV = −E · ds = 0 ⇒ E ⊥ ds
E = −∇V points the way V falls fastest. A contour is the way it does not change.
  • The sim finds the dashed tangent from the slope of V, and E from a separate sum of q/r² terms. They still meet at 90.0° at every point you try.
  • At (0, 1.50) for the dipole, E = 0.341 points along +x. The contour through that point is the y-axis, where V = 0.
  • For two like charges at the same point, E = 0.512 points straight up and the tangent lies flat.
See itSwitch q₂ to +, at (0, 1.50). Watch for: the amber arrow turning to point up, the dashed tangent lying flat, and the angle still reading 90.0°.
06

V = 0 does not mean E = 0

The cross-hair marks the midpoint, (0, 0). There V is a sum of numbers and E is a sum of arrows, and the two sums behave differently.

ChargesV(0, 0)|E(0, 0)|E points
+1 and −10.002.00from + to −
+1 and +12.000.00nowhere

For the dipole the two potentials, +1 and −1, cancel. Each charge's field points the same way, from + toward −, so the two fields add to 2. For like charges the potentials add to 2 and the two fields point opposite ways and cancel.

E depends on how fast V changes, not on its value. The chip gives both numbers, and the amber arrow shows E.

See itLook at the cross-hair for the dipole. Watch for: the chip reading V(0,0) = 0.00 and |E(0,0)| = 2.00, with an arrow pointing right.
See itSwitch q₂ to +. Watch for: the chip changing to V(0,0) = 2.00 and |E(0,0)| = 0.00, and the arrow disappearing.
07

Where it matters

  • Conductors. In electrostatics the surface of a conductor is an equipotential, so the field there meets the surface at right angles.
  • Contour maps. A hill map uses the same idea. Walking along a contour line does not change your height, and the steepest way up is at right angles to it.
  • Crowded rings. The faint rings step by equal ΔV, so rings that crowd mark a strong field, with |E| ≈ ΔV/Δr.
  • Careful. The counter reports the work you do for a unit positive test charge. It ignores any kinetic energy, so it is a statement about moving slowly.
08

Summary

In one line. A contour map shows where the potential has one value. Drag the charge across it and watch the work counter and the field arrow.

Key points

  • V is a scalar sum, V = q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂. An equipotential is a curve of constant V.
  • W = q ΔV, so moving along an equipotential takes no work.
  • E = −∇V, so E is perpendicular to the equipotential through every point.
  • V = 0 does not imply E = 0, and E = 0 does not imply V = 0.

Common mix-ups

  • "On an equipotential there is no field." The field is there, at right angles to the path.
  • "The work depends on the route." It depends only on V at the start and the end.
  • "Where V is zero, the field is zero." At the dipole midpoint V = 0 and |E| = 2.

Things to try on your own

  • Take a long trip and bring the counter back to 0.000.
  • Set q₂ to + and find a level with a contour in the frame, and one without.
  • Predict the angle at a point you choose, then check it.
